respect to criminal cases, that distinguishes between veracity, accuracy, and
reliability. Accuracy must be considered before one
finds the evidence to be reliable. Internal inconsistencies, external
inconsistencies, the harmony of the evidence with all of the other evidence in
the case, and whether or not there is evidence which is clearly indicative of
the fact that the witness is mistaken, wrong or inconsistent, must be looked at
in the assessment of the witness's testimony. See
R. v. Morrissey
,

1995 CanLII 3498 (ON CA)
, [
1995
] O. J. No. 639
.

[
250
]

In
R. v. H.C.
,
2009 ONCA 56 (CanLII)
,
[
2009
]
O. J. No. 214
,

the Ontario Court of Appeal noted that
credibility and reliability are two different matters. Credibility has to do
with a witness's veracity, whereas reliability has to do with the accuracy of
the witness' testimony. Accuracy requires a court to consider the ability of
the witness to accurately: observe, recall, and recount events in issue. Any
witness whose evidence on an issue is not credible cannot give reliable
evidence on the same point. However, credibility is not a proxy for
reliability: a credible witness may give unreliable evidence.

[
251
]

I appreciate that the case before this Court is
a civil case, which has a different standard of proof. Nevertheless, the
observations made by judges in criminal cases about assessing credibility are
pertinent to credibility assessment generally.

[
252
]

With respect to the first conversation alleged
by Ms. Kaffka and her husband, I am not able to conclude with any certainty
when it occurred and the precise nature of what was discussed. In assessing the
reliability of their evidence, I am troubled by the fact that something
apparently so important to Ms. Kaffka was not documented, or otherwise referred
to in the various electronic exchanges and chats between the parties. The
evidence generally established that there were ongoing communications between Ms.
Kaffka and Ms. Whitehall. On a balance of probabilities, I am not able to
conclude that Ms. Kaffka’s and Mr. Kaffka’s recollection of their discussion on
the speakerphone with Ms. Whitehall is entirely reliable. I do accept their
evidence that a telephone discussion took place. However, while I conclude it
is likely that an enhanced role for Ms. Kaffka was discussed, I cannot conclude
that Ms. Whitehall promised Ms. Kaffka co-ownership of the Film and any profits
that the Film might generate.

[
253
]

I now turn to the interaction of the parties on
May 25, 2017
,
on the telephone. In regard to that interaction, I do not
accept Ms. Whitehall’s assertion that she was “blackmailed” by Ms. Kaffka.
Further, I do not accept Ms. Whitehall’s description that Ms. Kaffka was
yelling and screaming, and was generally out of control. I prefer the evidence
of Ms. Bazuta who said that Ms. Kaffka was in no way rude to Ms. Whitehall
during that telephone conversation.

[
254
]

Both Ms. Kaffka and Mr. Kaffka testified that
during the telephone conversation, which occurred on May 25, 2017, Ms. Kaffka
told Ms. Whitehall that she wanted her agreement in writing. Ms. Kaffka
specifically said that she told Ms. Whitehall she wanted the co-executive
producer role clarified and she also wanted the co-ownership role clarified.
She said she wanted all of “this stuff” clarified in an email. Ms. Whitehall’s
response to Ms. Kaffka was that she was busy. She was at work but if Ms. Kaffka
sent her an email then she would email back an agreement.

[
255
]

Ms. Kaffka prepared an email and sent it to Ms.
Whitehall. In that email Ms. Kaffka in part wrote at the beginning of the
email, “To reiterate our phone call, I’m asking for co-executive producer
credit.” At the end she wrote, “If you agree to this, then we will move forward
with filming and I feel comfortable enough to come to a peaceful working
agreement with you.”

[
256
]

Minutes later Ms. Whitehall responded with an
email with just one word – “Agreed”. In her direct evidence, Ms. Whitehall gave
an explanation about what she thought before she sent that one word answer. She
said first of all she was shocked by Ms. Kaffka’s outburst. Then she thought
about the fact that there were actors and crew who had booked the weekend off
to work on the Film project. According to Ms. Whitehall, she did not want the
Film shut down because a lot of people were expected on set. She also thought
that it was co-executive producer “credit” and was not “executive producer”.
She was the executive producer. She then drew a parallel in her thinking, to
the effect that executive producer is like the president and co-executive
producer is like the vice president. Ms. Whitehall concluded they were not
equal roles. She also rationalized it (that is my conclusion and not Ms.
Whitehall’s words) by saying that it was strictly a film credit. That it was
very common in the film industry. It is like a bit of a bonus and it is a
gesture. After having thought all of that, Ms. Whitehall agreed to the credit
as “co-executive producer”. Ms. Whitehall said that no other terms were
discussed during that phone call. According to Ms. Whitehall’s recollection, it
was after the phone call and her agreement that she received a flurry of emails
or at least that is how her evidence came across.

[
257
]

It appears from Ms. Whitehall’s evidence in
direct that while she was receiving the emails from Ms. Kaffka, she was also on
the phone with her friend who was a social worker. That was because, according
to Ms. Whitehall, she was “so distraught”. She was reading the emails from Ms.
Kaffka to her friend as they were coming in and asking her friend what she
should do. Should she shut down the filming? Should she call Ms. Kaffka’s
bluff? When Ms. Whitehall testified, she said in hindsight that is probably
what she should have done.

[
258
]

Ms. Kaffka responded to Ms. Whitehall saying,
“Thank you. Now let’s go make a great film this weekend and let all of this
go.” About half an hour later, Ms. Whitehall replied saying that she never
wanted to fight with Ms. Kaffka. Ms. Whitehall said she was surprised that they
“got to such an ugly place.” She also said that they should move forward in
peace. Ms. Whitehall noted they had a huge and amazing cast and crew and that
it was going to be a great film.

[
259
]

This Court needs to determine whether the above
noted exchanges establish that, in addition to granting Ms. Kaffka the
co-executive producer title/credit, Ms. Whitehall also granted or confirmed
that she was granting co-ownership. Both Ms. Kaffka and her husband say that is
what was discussed in the telephone call on May 25, 2017. However, Ms. Kaffka’s
email to Ms. Whitehall does not mention co-ownership. Ms. Kaffka was asked why
she did not put that in her email. Ms. Kaffka said she did not do so because
she was happy to just get something in writing at the time. She thought that
her co-ownership would flow with the credit. Ms. Kaffka did not think she
needed to clarify that point (about co-ownership) because Ms. Whitehall was
admitting to this and putting it in writing. Given the issues that Ms. Kaffka
described in relation to getting additional recognition and getting it in
writing, I find her evidence in this regard puzzling and somewhat perplexing.
More importantly, it is at odds with Ms. Kaffka’s stated objective that she
wanted their earlier agreement in writing and as well wanted the co-executive
producer role to be clarified. Ms. Kaffka testified she wanted everything clarified
in an email.

[
260
]

The only other person who was not related to the
parties and who was present for the phone call is Ms. Bazuta. Her testimony was
that she heard both sides of the conversation. She said there was talk about Ms.
Kaffka being given credit for being the director and as well co-executive
producer. It was her understanding that these were things that had been
promised in previous discussions. However, it was clear that Ms. Bazuta had no
direct knowledge of any of the previous discussions, except what she was told
by Ms. Kaffka. In an undated letter of support that Ms. Bazuta at some point
prepared, she wrote that she was aware Ms. Kaffka was the producer, executive
producer, and director on the Film project. Ms. Bazuta did not mention
co-ownership in her evidence. Further, although she mentioned hearing reference
to co-executive producer credit, she did not mention that in the letter of
support she subsequently sent.

[
261
]

I am satisfied that there was discussion during
the telephone call of May 25, 2017, between Ms. Kaffka and Ms. Whitehall, which
ended with Ms. Kaffka sending a one word reply, namely, “Agreed”. That reply
was to an email Ms. Whitehall asked Ms. Kaffka to write to her. The only
substantive role mentioned in that email was that of co-executive producer. I
find there can be no dispute that Ms. Whitehall agreed to give Ms. Kaffka that
title. It is interesting to note the effort Ms. Whitehall made to minimize the
importance of giving that title to Ms. Kaffka. I do not accept Ms. Whitehall’s
evidence that it meant as little as she thought it did. Earlier in her
testimony and in final submissions both Ms. Whitehall and her counsel focused
on the importance of credits, and emphasized that a credit in a short film production
is significant enough to be consideration, in the legal sense. Ms. Whitehall
cannot have it both ways. It cannot be a mere gesture in one case, i.e. when
she granted the title co-executive producer to Ms. Kaffka, and yet significant
enough to constitute consideration for the contract/agreement Ms. Whitehall
maintains existed with respect to the roles of director/producer. Whether
anything will turn on this on other matters in this case is yet to be
determined. However, it is important to note that what Ms. Whitehall “thought”
was not ever communicated to Ms. Kaffka and thus Ms. Whitehall’s subjective
intention can be given no weight.

[
262
]

Nevertheless, in respect to whether Ms.
Whitehall also agreed to give Ms. Kaffka co-ownership and profits, I find that the
defendants have not satisfied me through their evidence, that such an agreement
was reached. As I noted in respect to the first telephone call sometime in
April 2017, it is difficult to understand why there is no documentation of such
an important issue. In this instance there was at least some documentation,
namely, the email Ms. Kaffka sent in response to Ms. Whitehall’s request. That
email, however, only refers to co-executive producer credit. Moreover, Ms. Bazuta,
the independent witness who heard both sides of the conversation could only
confirm that co-executive producer credit was discussed. She did not mention
co-ownership or profits. Accordingly, I cannot conclude, on the basis of the
evidence available, that in addition to reaching an agreement about the co-executive
producer credit, Ms. Kaffka and Ms. Whitehall also reached an agreement
regarding co-ownership and profits. Therefore, I am not satisfied that such an
agreement about co-ownership and profits was established on the evidence.

Was Ms. Kaffka a maker
and/or co-author of the Film?

[
263
]

The defendants submit that the Film, on its own,
is an original work and is distinguishable from the Script. They submit that Ms.
Kaffka undertook the necessary arrangements, and contributed substantial skill,
judgment, and creativity to turn the Script into another work, namely, the
Film. They submit that through Ms. Kaffka’s creative, financial, and in-kind
contributions, separate from her role as director and producer, she provided
more than mere ideas and suggestions for the Film. Accordingly, they submit Ms.
Kaffka is a joint author and maker of the Film and thereby is an owner within
the meaning of the
Copyright Act
.

[
264
]

There was considerable evidence about the amount
of additional work, over and above her roles as director and producer, which Ms.
Kaffka did in preparation for shooting the Film. That additional work included:
working on finding locations, revising the Script, setting up social media
platforms and revising the budget. Ms. Kaffka did not do this alone as Ms.
Whitehall worked on some of those matters as well. Additionally, Ms. Kaffka
organized equipment for the Film, booked the majority of the crew, arranged for
catering and craft services, arranged for set decorations and props and also
made some, and worked with heads of departments. Further, Ms. Kaffka provided
both financial (which the claimants say were unsolicited) and in-kind
contributions. She also provided industry contacts.

[
265
]

As noted by the defendants, the term “author” is
not defined in the
Copyright Act
. However, in
Glasz c. Choko
,

2018 QCCS 5020
, the court noted that the case law recognizes an author as the
person who exercised skill and judgment to express an idea and to fix it in
material form. In this case, the defendants submit that Ms. Kaffka worked
collaboratively with Ms. Whitehall on the Film and that their collaborative
work resulted in a work of joint authorship.

[
266
]

In
Seggie c. Roofdog Games Inc
.,
2015
QCCS 6462
, the court relied on s. 2 of the
Copyright Act
and on certain
principles, which are set out below, to determine whether a video game was a
work of joint authorship. Section 2 defines a work of joint authorship as, “a
work produced by the collaboration of two or more authors in which the
contribution of one author is not distinct from the contribution of the other
author or authors.”

[
267
]

The principles distilled from the case law to
apply in determining whether a work is created by joint authors are as follows:

•

a work will be considered to have been created
jointly on the basis of the
Copyright Act
and the facts,

•           the
contribution of the co-authors need not be equivalent, but the contribution of
each must be substantial,

•           there must
have been some collaboration between the co-authors in the pursuit of a common
design,

•           it is
necessary to prove more than ideas and suggestions, and

•           whether or
not the parties had a common intention to create a work of joint authorship.

[
268
]

As previously noted, the claimants dispute and
deny that Ms. Kaffka and Ms. Whitehall entered into any kind of business
venture, including joint authorship. They reiterate their position that Ms.
Whitehall engaged Ms. Kaffka on behalf of Whitehall Entertainment to direct and
produce the Film. In addition to this general denial of any kind of business
venture, the claimants submit a further principle to be considered when
addressing whether a work is one of joint authorship is found in
Neudorf v.
Nettwerk Productions Ltd
.,
1999 CanLII 7014
(BCSC). In that decision at paragraph
95 the court agreed with the statement, contained in a U.S. decision, that a
person should not be elevated to the status of joint author unless each of the
collaborators intended the other to be a joint author of the work.

[
269
]

In their argument, the defendants urge this
Court to essentially untether the making of the Film from the Script. The
defendants rely on the Scottish case
Milligan v.

Broadway Cinema Ltd.

(1923), 1920 3S LT 35, for the proposition that when determining the ownership
of a cinematographic work, the focus of the inquiry must be on the
cinematographic work itself and not on the underlying work.

[
270
]

I conclude, in the circumstances and on the
evidence before me, that the approach in
Milligan
is not an appropriate
one to apply. Additionally, I must be careful when reviewing foreign cases and
applying them in the Canadian context. In this case, we have a very short film
with virtually no dialogue, except through dialogue cards. The Film is only
approximately 18 minutes long and, as far as I can discern from the evidence
submitted, it is substantially based on the Script. That point alone raises the
question of whether the Film, on its own, qualifies as an original work. It is
clear, that the reason the defendants wish to establish that Ms. Kaffka was an
author or a maker is because the author or a maker of an original work is the
first owner of the copyright in that work.

[
271
]

In
CCH

Canadian Ltd.
the Supreme
Court of Canada reviewed some basic principles regarding copyright law. Those
principles are:

a)         Copyright
under the
Copyright Act
subsists in every original literary, dramatic,
musical and artistic work. Accordingly, originality sets the boundaries of
copyright law. However, the term “original” is not defined in the
Act
.

b)         After
reviewing competing views on the meaning of “original”, the Court concluded
that neither the “sweat of the brow” or “industriousness” standard of
originality nor the “creativity” approach to originality is applicable in
Canada. Instead, the Court concluded that the correct position falls between
those two extremes.

c)         Therefore, for
a work to be “original” within the meaning of the
Act
it must be more
than a mere copy of another work. It need not be creative in the sense of being
novel or unique, but there must be exercise of skill and judgment. By “skill”
the Court meant the use of one’s knowledge, developed aptitude, or practised
ability in producing the work. By “judgment “the Court meant the use of one’s
capacity for discernment or ability to form an opinion or evaluation by
comparing different possible options in producing the work.

d)         The Court
specifically concluded that an “original” work under the
Copyright Act

is one that originates from an author and is not copied from another work.
However, in addition an original work must be the product of the author’s
exercise of skill and judgment.

[
272
]

Ms. Kaffka testified that she made suggestions
and other changes to the Script between the time when she first received it in
March 2017 and when the Film shoot was done. In fact, she also testified that
she had to make some changes on the fly the first day of shooting. They were
told they did not have permission to film at a flower shop. So she ended up
having to rewrite the scene and move the shooting of the scene elsewhere.
However,

given Ms. Kaffka’s concession that she is not claiming
copyright in the Script, the suggestions and the revisions she may have made to
the Script are not a factor that can be properly considered in determining
whether she is an author or co-author of the Film.

[
273
]

Several copies of the Script were filed by both
parties as exhibits. My understanding of the evidence is that the basic
storyline, including the sequence and the order of the “scenes” and other
details in the story arc, did not change substantially from the Script, which Ms.
Kaffka received from Ms. Whitehall.

[
274
]

The defendants submit that over and above Ms.
Kaffka’s obligations as a director and producer, Ms. Kaffka provided creative,
financial and in-kind contributions. Accordingly, they argue that Ms. Kaffka
should be considered a maker and/or joint author of the Film as she took the
necessary arrangements, and contributed substantial skill, judgment and
creativity to turn the Script into a new original work, namely, the Film.

[
275
]

There is no doubt that Ms. Kaffka and Ms.
Whitehall worked collaboratively, until the latter stages leading up to the
filming weekend. There is also no doubt that in her role as director and
producer Ms. Kaffka made important contributions in turning the Script into the
Film. However, on the evidence before this Court, I am not able to conclude that
Ms. Kaffka’s contributions represent the kind of exercise of skill and judgment
that is required for Ms. Kaffka to be considered an author or co-author of the
Film. A similar conclusion was reached in
Andrews
,
albeit in the context
of a copyright dispute regarding a software system.

[
276
]

Additionally, and more importantly, the evidence
in this case does not establish that the parties, in particular Ms. Kaffka and
Ms. Whitehall, had a common intention to create a work of joint authorship.
Accordingly, I do not find that Ms. Kaffka was a maker/author of an original
work which was distinguishable from the Script.

Did the
parties enter into a joint venture?

[
277
]

In the alternative, the defendants submit that Ms.
Kaffka is a co-owner of the Film as a result of a common undertaking or joint venture
she and Ms. Whitehall entered into to make the Script into the Film. The
defendants submit that a joint venture must have a contractual basis. However,
it need not be reduced to writing. The defendants further submit that the
contractual basis for the joint venture in this case is the agreement reached
in the telephone conversation sometime in

April 2017, between Ms.
Whitehall and Ms. Kaffka, the subsequent conversation on May 25, 2017, and Ms.
Whitehall’s May 25, 2017, reply.

[
278
]

In
Canlan Investment Corp. v. Gettling
,
1997 CanLII 4126 (BC CA)
, [1997]
B.C.J. No. 1647, the Court identified the factors which underlie a joint
venture as follows:

•

a contribution by the parties of money,
property, effort, knowledge, skill or other asset to a common undertaking,

•

a joint property interest in the subject matter
of the venture,

•

a right of mutual control or management of the
enterprise,

•

an expectation of profit or the presence of adventure
as it is sometimes called,

•

a right to participate in the profits, and

•

a limitation of the objective to a single
undertaking or
ad hoc
enterprise. (See paragraphs 33 to 35)

[
279
]

The defendants submit that Ms. Whitehall
admitted there was a common goal with an expectation of awards and recognition.
Moreover, the other factors identified in the case law are also met in this
instance.

[
280
]

The claimants submit that Ms. Whitehall’s
acknowledgement that it was a common goal of Ms. Whitehall and Ms. Kaffka to
complete the Film should be viewed in context. That context is that the
production of every film is a collaborative effort among many people who make
up the cast and crew. They say it would be an absurd result to conclude that by
simply having the common goal of turning a script into a film, everyone with
such a common goal would be granted ownership in a film.

[
281
]

The claimants rely on a U.S. case
16 Casa
Duse, LLC v. Alex Merkin & Maurice A.

Reichman
No. 13 – 3868.
That case dealt with competing claims between a director of a film, who had not
signed a written contract, and the production company. In that case, the U.S.
Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit found that a director’s contribution to
an integrated “work of authorship”, such as a film, is not itself a “work of
authorship” subject to its own copyright protection. The court further found
that only the “dominant author” would own copyright.

[
282
]

In
Compo Co.
,
the Court recognized that
U.S. copyright cases may not be easily transferable to Canada because there are
key differences in the copyright concepts in Canadian and American copyright
legislation. The fact of the differences between the two jurisdictions was
again noted by the Supreme Court of Canada in
CCH

Canadian Ltd.

in 2004, and a judge of the Federal Court also commented on the differences in
Andrews
.

Accordingly, caution dictates that it is not prudent to apply the analysis
in
16 Casa Duse
to the case before this Court.

[
283
]

I acknowledge the defendants’ point that
although a joint venture must have a contractual basis it does not need to be
in writing. Of course, the existence of a written agreement would have gone a
long way to establishing the parties’ intentions and points of agreement
regarding the joint venture. In this case, the evidence supports a conclusion
that both Ms. Whitehall and Ms. Kaffka made contributions to the making of the
Film. However, Ms. Kaffka’s monetary contributions did not appear to have been
discussed with Ms. Whitehall or part of a common understanding between Ms.
Whitehall and Ms. Kaffka. Moreover, given Ms. Kaffka’s concession that she did
not own the Script and my conclusions above that Ms. Kaffka did not obtain
ownership or co-ownership by agreement or as a joint author, Ms. Whitehall and Ms.
Kaffka do not have a joint property interest in the subject matter of the
venture, namely, the Film.

[
284
]

Additionally, given the disputes that have
arisen between Ms. Whitehall and Ms. Kaffka and the absence of any formal
agreement, I find it difficult to conclude that there was a right of mutual
control or management over the enterprise. That may well have been Ms. Kaffka’s
perception (at least in the early stages of their relationships), but that view
was not shared by Ms. Whitehall who throughout the trial was at pains to
describe herself in leadership roles and to distance herself from the roles
filled by Ms. Kaffka. In sum, I am unable to find that Ms. Kaffka is a co-owner
of the Film arising from a common undertaking or joint venture with Ms.
Whitehall and/or Whitehall Entertainment to turn the Script into a Film.

[
285
]

In conclusion, for the reasons set out above, I
find that the defences raised by Ms. Kaffka to establish ownership and thereby
right to copyright do not apply in the circumstances of this case. However, I
do find that Ms. Whitehall agreed to give Ms. Kaffka the title “co- executive
producer” and the credits that go with it.

Was infringement established through the
specific activities?

[
286
]

The claimants have identified specific
activities by which they say the infringement occurred. They maintain that any
of the activities they identified, after the shooting weekend, namely, May 27
and 28, 2017, were either wrongful under contract or tort law or were an
infringement under the
Copyright Act
. However, it appears that failing
to return certain items and failing to provide a copy of the edited Film are allegations
that do not fall within the infringement provisions of the
Copyright Act.

[
287
]

The documentary evidence establishes that very
shortly after the filming, on June 1, 2017, Ms. Kaffka forwarded some invoices
to Ms. Whitehall. She wrote that she did not have a lot of time that weekend
because she was “wrapping out”. Ms. Whitehall wrote back several hours later
requesting a specific lighting invoice. In that email, she wrote to Ms. Kaffka
that they needed to talk. Ms. Whitehall stated she was the executive producer,
whether Ms. Kaffka liked it or not, and they needed to communicate to get the
project finished. Ms. Whitehall wrote that she was going to update the budget
and would send an email to Ms. Kaffka so that they could cross-reference
everything to make sure everyone was paid. Ms. Whitehall also wrote that she
wanted to talk to Ms. Kaffka about something that had happened in her apartment
at the end of the shoot with a crew member.

[
288
]

Ms. Kaffka responded almost immediately and
noted that she had never said they would not talk. She explained that she was
“wrapping out” and did not have a lot of time. She further suggested that going
forward their communications should be by email to avoid miscommunication.
However, Ms. Kaffka noted that if the incident Ms. Whitehall raised was
sensitive, she would call her. Approximately 90 minutes later, Ms. Kaffka wrote
to Ms. Whitehall again noting that the two of them were co-executive producers
and that Ms. Whitehall was not her boss and never had been. She asked Ms. Whitehall
to ask her nicely if she wanted to meet or have her call, instead of attempting
to order her around. Ms. Kaffka also said she was tired of Ms. Whitehall’s
tone. She was a human being who had worked hard on the project and not Ms.
Whitehall’s lackey or whipping post.

[
289
]

Ms. Whitehall responded later in the evening
writing that Ms. Kaffka had been completely inappropriate with her. She wrote
that Ms. Kaffka had been abusive on the phone on Thursday (presumably May 25).
She also said they were not co-executive producers. Ms. Whitehall wrote she was
the executive producer. She continued the email saying that Ms. Kaffka had been
a nightmare to work with and that she was fed up with Ms. Kaffka’s tone, her
yelling, her disrespect, and her accusations. She told Ms. Kaffka to take some
personal responsibility. She also said that Ms. Kaffka owed her an apology and
that Ms. Kaffka’s behaviour was outrageous. Ms. Whitehall ended the email by
saying that she had never worked with anyone so unprofessional in her life.

[
290
]

The following day June 2, 2017, Ms. Kaffka wrote
back to Ms. Whitehall. She pointed out that Ms. Whitehall had done nothing but
talk down to everyone and make demands that were unreasonable. She wrote that
Ms. Whitehall had been oblivious to the real costs and work associated with the
Film and had done very little to contribute. Ms. Kaffka also wrote that she did
not yell at Ms. Whitehall nor was she abusive. Ms. Kaffka said she simply
defended herself against someone who was pushing her around. She pointed out
that Ms. Whitehall’s financial contribution of $8,000 did not make the Film
happen. Instead, Ms. Kaffka said it was her contacts and her resources that
made the Film happen.

[
291
]

In the June 2, 2017, email Ms. Kaffka listed
what the cash and in-kind contributions were, as well as what had been
contributed by the crew she brought in for labour and so on. Ms. Kaffka ended
the email with a proposal, which was that she would pay for an additional shoot
day and the additional labour as promised. She would deliver the director’s cut
of the Film to Ms. Whitehall to view and the two of them could meet with Zakim
Nuraney together to hear his ideas. They would then modify as needed and send
the Film to be scored. Ms. Kaffka further wrote that the final Film would be
delivered to Ms. Whitehall for her to market as she wished. Ms. Kaffka wrote
she would take a copy of the Film for her portfolio only.

[
292
]

In the email, Ms. Kaffka also set out terms to
go with her proposal. She wanted to make sure that: Ms. Whitehall would not
remove her access to the Facebook page; she would be given access to all social
media accounts associated with the Film that existed or were created in the
future; she would help to promote the project; Ms. Whitehall would not remove
her name as director or co-executive producer at any point in the future; she
would send a zip file of all the production documents to Ms. Whitehall but they
were not to be modified; she would be told about screenings and festivals and
be able to attend to represent the Film if she wished; and she would be invited
to the official premiere or crew screening. Ms. Kaffka noted that if they were
not able to come to an arrangement or if the agreement they reached was reneged
on in the future, she would inform her entertainment lawyer to arrange for
mediation. She also wrote that other than that Ms. Whitehall could do what she
wished with the Film.

[
293
]

The next email communication was from Ms.
Whitehall to Ms. Kaffka on the morning of June 5, 2017. Ms. Whitehall wrote it
was unfortunate that they had gotten to “this terrible place in our working
relationship” but she thought they shared a common goal of wanting to complete
the Film. Ms. Whitehall said she would agree to the following: she would give Ms.
Kaffka co-executive producer credit after the Film was completed but on the
condition that it was for credit purposes only and that it did not give Ms.
Kaffka any rights or ownership of the Film; Whitehall Entertainment would
retain one hundred percent of the ownership and control of the Film as well as
marketing and promotion; she would keep Ms. Kaffka updated on the Film’s
acceptance in film festivals; Ms. Kaffka would be invited to local screenings
and was welcome to represent the Film at her own expense at international
screenings; Ms. Whitehall would forward any social media correspondence
addressed to the director to Ms. Kaffka for response; Ms. Kaffka would receive
credits as director and producer as originally agreed upon; and Whitehall
Entertainment would pay for the additional filming day to a maximum of $1,000.

[
294
]

In the June 5 email Ms. Whitehall noted that she
needed to work with Ms. Kaffka and Matt Popp, first assistant director, to help
prioritize the shots since they were working on a very tight budget. She
thought they would be able to streamline what was outstanding and work with the
existing footage. Ms. Whitehall said she would not interfere with Ms. Kaffka’s
directing, as she had not during the shooting of the Film. Ms. Whitehall said
all she was asking was that Ms. Kaffka collaborate with her in advance to see
what really needed to be filmed for the sake of the storyline. Ms. Whitehall
also noted that since Ms. Kaffka was viewing a rough edit that day, Ms. Kaffka
would have a good understanding of how to guide the film to completion with the
additional shots. The next condition was that Ms. Whitehall would review the director’s
cut and provide notes.

[
295
]

It appears there were further communications by
email between the parties. In a letter that Ms. Kaffka sent to Ms. Whitehall’s
lawyer, on or about June 20, 2017, Ms. Kaffka noted she had sent an email to
Ms. Whitehall that the director of photography was not available on June 11,
the date that everyone else was available for the additional shoot. In that
email Ms. Kaffka wrote that she would email Ms. Whitehall as soon as there was
a new date.

[
296
]

On June 16, 2017, two letters were sent to Ms.
Kaffka. One letter was from Whitehall Entertainment, signed by Ms. Whitehall.
In that letter Ms. Kaffka was notified that Whitehall Entertainment terminated
her “engagement” effective immediately as director and co-producer and of all
related services provided by her for the Film. Ms. Kaffka was asked to return
all property related to the Film including costumes, canvases, yoga mat no
later than June 20, 2017. Ms. Kaffka was also advised that two different
amounts had been sent to her via e-transfer which were for petty cash and craft
services and all monies not accounted for should be reimbursed to Whitehall
Entertainment.

[
297
]

The second letter was signed by Harvey Meller
who represented Whitehall Entertainment and Ms. Whitehall. That letter
contained a recitation of the details of the agreement as relayed to Mr. Meller
by his clients. It also referred to the attached letter from Whitehall
Entertainment, presumably the termination letter mentioned above. Mr. Meller
wrote that Ms. Kaffka had denied Ms. Whitehall involvement in the creation of
the Film in both the preparation of additional shooting days and prioritizing
shot lists. He maintained that Ms. Whitehall had requested involvement on
multiple occasions. The client was of the view that Ms. Kaffka was not prepared
to allow Ms. Whitehall proper involvement in the shooting, editing and
completion of the Film. Additionally, Mr. Meller wrote it appeared Ms. Kaffka
had been unable to complete the Film in the time allotted and in accordance
with the agreed budget. He ended the recitation saying that for all of those
reasons and as a result of “irreconcilable differences” between Ms. Kaffka and
Ms. Whitehall, Whitehall Entertainment had chosen to terminate her engagement
as director and co-producer of the Film.

[
298
]

Mr. Meller’s letter went on to say that,
notwithstanding the termination, Ms. Whitehall on her own behalf and on behalf
of Whitehall Entertainment affirmed their agreement to honour all of the
promises to Ms. Kaffka and detailed what those promises were. The letter also
said that in addition Ms. Whitehall and Whitehall Entertainment agreed to
provide Ms. Kaffka a co-executive producer credit upon execution of an attached
release, waiver, and transfer agreement.

The alleged specific infringements

[
299
]

The specific infringements the fall under the
Copyright
Act
, which were alleged by the claimants are:

a)         editing raw
footage used to create the Film without Ms. Whitehall’s input,

b)         screening the
Film to crew members without authority,

c)         posting the
Film or clips thereof on social media/online sites,

d)         submitting the
director’s cut of the Film to several film festivals,

e)         marketing/promoting
the director’s cut online.

Editing raw Film footage

[
300
]

I turn first to editing of the raw footage. In
this regard, I first need to address the time frame asserted by the claimants.
They maintain that anything done after the shooting weekend, May 27 and 28, was
done without permission and is the basis for their infringement claims. I find,
given the evidence before this Court, and in particular the documentary
evidence of communications between Ms. Kaffka and Ms. Whitehall after the
shooting weekend, that the activities Ms. Kaffka initially carried out after
May 28, 2017, fall under the implied licence that was granted by the
defendants. While the personal relationship between Ms. Kaffka and Ms.
Whitehall was fraught with difficulties, there is no clear evidence that her
responsibilities as a director and producer, or for that matter as co-executive
producer, had ended. The evidence is that by the time her engagement was
formally “terminated” on June 16, 2017, Ms. Kaffka had already edited a rough
cut of the Film.

[
301
]

Ms. Kaffka said Ms. Whitehall was away for about
two or three weeks right after the filming. However, they had agreed that Ms.
Kaffka would do a director’s cut, which would be submitted to the film
festivals. Therefore, Ms. Kaffka went ahead and did everything as she normally
would. Her view in this regard is supported by the fact that when Ms. Whitehall
wrote letters to the crew and cast members after shooting the Film, in
particular on or about May 31 and June 1, 2017, Ms. Whitehall specifically
referred to looking forward to the private screening on July 23, 2017. In one
email she also mentioned that “the bike” would be needed because some follow-up
shots were necessary. This was in keeping with Ms. Kaffka’s understanding both
about the festivals and about continuing to work on the Film.

[
302
]

Ms. Kaffka testified that she went through the
process of getting the Film edited as she normally would. In fact she
specifically said that we (referring to Zakim Nuraney and Shawn Seifert) went
right to the editing room and started going through the footage. Ms. Kaffka
went into some detail about what she did post-production. She explained that
there was going to be some extensive visual effects work (adding colour or
pulling out colour for certain objects and certain other things). Accordingly,
they cut any extra things out of the Film. The clear implication was that this
occurred while she was involved with the edits to the Film. Ms. Kaffka wanted
to get all that done before any re-shooting took place because she did not want
to do any extra unnecessary filming.

[
303
]

Ms. Kaffka said that she just went about getting
the Film edited. She went through different versions with Zakim Nuraney. In
that regard, I note the by the time that the claimants’ lawyer wrote to Mr.
Nuraney, he had already returned the hard drives that contained the Film he had
edited to Ms. Kaffka. There was no cross-examination on this point or specifically
about the dates when Ms. Kaffka was involved in the editing process. Ms. Kaffka
sent a note to some cast members on June 1, 2017, with a copy to Ms. Whitehall.
That email set out the scenes/inserts that needed to be completed. In that
email she specifically said that she would look at the “draft edit” the
following Monday. Clearly, it appears from that email that the edit or draft
edit, as she called it, was underway at that time.

[
304
]

There was an exchange of correspondence with Mr.
Nuraney submitted by the claimants.

On June 16, 2017, Mr. Meller wrote
to Mr. Nuraney and advised that Ms. Kaffka had been terminated. The letter to
Mr. Nuraney also said Whitehall Entertainment was going to engage a new crew to
complete the Film. It asked Mr. Nuraney to deliver all hard drives, cables and
cords. It asked him to include
all edited footage
and upon receiving it
they would pay him any remaining compensation that had been promised to him.
They also promised that they would provide credit for his services as DIT and
editor. The deadline for providing all of the materials was June 19, 2017.

[
305
]

Mr. Nuraney responded on June 17, 2017, in the
early afternoon. He wrote that the situation came as a shock to him. He had
currently logged in 83 hours into the Film. He had not yet been paid his full
editing fee of $400 or given credit for it. He did not understand what was
going on. He also noted that since wrapping production he had worked closely
with Ms. Kaffka on the edit. He also commented this was standard fare in the
process of making a film. He said before any hand-off happened he wanted to be
paid in full and wanted to see his credits for the project. He said that he
also logged in a number of hours for visual

effects (VFX).There was
further email correspondence with Mr. Nuraney, who wrote back on June 21, 2017,
that he was not in possession of the hard drives. He had edited the Film at Ms.
Kaffka’s place.

[
306
]

Mr. Nuraney’s correspondence suggests that the
editing may have been largely completed by the time the termination letter was
sent to Ms. Kaffka on June 16, 2017, or shortly thereafter. It appears from the
letter that Mr. Meller sent to Mr. Nuraney, requesting all the edited footage that
he and his client believed the editing was done. A further inference I draw
from the evidence is that much, if not all, of the editing had been done well
before the July 10, 2017, cease-and-desist letter. However, Ms. Kaffka, in
answer to a question in direct, said that the Film was complete by August 1,
presumably 2017. There was no cross-examination on that point or what it meant
in terms of any additional editing after the editing done immediately
post-production. Additionally, there was an email in the exhibits dated March
6, 2018, from Ms Kaffka, which lists approximately 15 items that needed
editing. I do not know quite what to make of that as I do not recall any specific
evidence about what editing the items listed in that email entailed.

[
307
]

My review of the evidence leads me to conclude Ms.
Kaffka participated in the film editing process. Her evidence was that Mr.
Nuraney was doing the actual editing of the Film and another person Shawn
Seifert was advising/assisting. The evidence establishes that in early June
2017, Ms. Kaffka was working to a deadline of sorts because they were planning
to shoot pickup shots on June 10 or 11, 2017. Moreover, there is also evidence
from Mr. Nuraney’ s  emails that by June 17, 2017, he had put in about 83 hours,
which appears to refer to editing. He said he had worked on the editing with Ms.
Kaffka since immediately after the Film shooting and this was standard.

[
308
]

There was no evidence pointed out to me, given
on the claimants’ behalf, which specified the time frame when the impugned editing
was done. Despite my findings that Ms. Kaffka was involved in the editing
process post-production, I cannot conclude on the evidence before this Court
that Ms. Kaffka personally did any editing after she received the termination
letter dated June 16, 2017.

[
309
]

It is notable that in a subsequent letter dated
July 10, 2017, from Mr. Meller it is specifically noted “… For greater clarity
you may not continue to shoot, edit, release, exhibit, publish or cause to be
published or register or cause to be registered copyright in your name or any
name...” The June 16, 2017, letter terminating her engagement only referred to “related
services”. Editing was not specifically mentioned. It is also only in the
letter of July 10, 2017, that counsel demanded Ms. Kaffka, “cease and desist
all actions relating to the production of this version of
Hey, That’s My
Bike!
’ (‘the Film’), and hereby demand return of all hard drives related to
the Film…”

[
310
]

Nevertheless, while there is little specific
evidence that points to Ms. Kaffka personally editing the Film after having
been specifically put on notice not to do so, she was definitely involved in
the editing process.  I have already pointed out the email she sent to Shawn Seifert
on March 6, 2018, listing a number of things that needed editing.

The evidence is not clear as to

what
editing, if any, was done after that email was sent. It is possible that some
editing was done. Ms. Kaffka’s own evidence is that the Film was not completed
until August 1. The significance of this is that although Ms. Kaffka likely
worked on the editing process immediately after the shooting of the Film (while
she was still  performing her role as director and producer ) she continued to
do so after receiving the termination letter and after the July 10, 2017,
cease-and-desist letter was sent to her.

[
311
]

Therefore, I find

on a balance of
probabilities, that the claimants have established copyright infringement. They
have established that Ms. Kaffka continued to be involved in the editing
process up to the beginning of August 2017 and likely in some minor editing on
or about the spring of 2018. On the basis of the evidence adduced I can only
conclude that the majority of the editing was done when Mr. Nuraney worked on
it with Ms. Kaffka shortly after the shooting weekend. However, it is clear
that some more editing or other work was done in order for the Film to be
“completed” on August 1, 2017.

Screening the Film

[
312
]

I now turn to the allegation that Ms. Kaffka
committed an infringement under the
Copyright Act
by screening the Film.
Ms. Kaffka was asked to comment on evidence given by Ms. Matzov that there was
a film screening at a pub on Granville Street. That evidence arose in
cross-examination when Ms. Matzov was asked why Ms. Kaffka was not listed as
executive producer in any credits relating to the Film. Ms. Matzov said she
thought Ms. Kaffka was listed in the credits, but she had not seen the Film
since 2017. Ms. Matzov said that she believed Ms. Kaffka was credited, meaning
the end credits, as producer.

[
313
]

Ms. Matzov was asked which version of the Film
she had seen. She said it was the first version. She did not know there were
multiple versions. Claimant’s counsel also asked where she had seen it. Ms. Matzov
said the best she could recall was that the screening was at a bar on Granville
Street. Ms. Matzov believed that the screening had been organized by Ms. Kaffka.
Ms. Matzov’s recollection was tentative and clearly negatively affected by the
passage of time.

[
314
]

Ms. Kaffka testified that Ms. Matzov had worked
with her on another film after the Film. Ms. Kaffka said there was a screening
for that film sometime later. It had nothing to do with the Film in issue. Ms.
Kaffka had also been invited to a wrap party that was given by Crystal Lowe and
Ashley Alexander in relation to other films. Ms. Kaffka testified it was a

wrap

party but there was no screening of any films. Ms. Kaffka specifically
testified that at no point did she have a wrap party during which the Film was
screened.

[
315
]

In the circumstances, I accept the evidence of Ms.
Kaffka that she did not have a party at which she screened the Film.
Accordingly, on the issue of a screening at a party at a bar/pub on Granville
Street, I find that the claimants have not established this alleged
infringement.

[
316
]

The claimants also assert that there was an
unauthorized screening/posting of a cut of the Film to certain members of the
crew. This point could be raised either under posting or screening. I have
chosen to address it under screening for convenience. Ms. Kaffka acknowledged
that she uploaded the completed Film to Vimeo. This was a password-protected
upload. Her email about this dated June 4, 2018, was addressed to the cast and
the crew. However, it is unclear whether all the cast was actually included. Ms.
Kaffka wrote there would not be an official screening and she wanted them to
see what their hard work had created. She noted that the link would expire by
midnight the following day. In her testimony, Ms. Kaffka said she also put the
Film that was on Vimeo on her personal Facebook page because a few people were
not able to view it on Vimeo. That link was available for approximately 12
hours and was password protected. Although Ms. Kaffka acknowledged those
postings, she maintained she did not post the Film anywhere for public viewing.
Ms. Kaffka had privacy settings in place so that only the people she invited
could see the Film.

[
317
]

I was not directed to any definition of
“posting” or “screening” or “public” in the
Act
. However, there is a
definition of “publication”. That definition, found at s. 2.2 of the
Act

states that in relation to works, “publication” means making copies of the work
available to the public. I further note that s. 3 (1) (d) of the
Act
provides

that copyright, in the case of a dramatic work, includes the right to
reproduce, adapt and publicly present the work as a cinematographic work.

[
318
]

In this instance, the Film was posted on Ms.
Kaffka’s personal website and on Vimeo. Access for both was password protected.
The posting of the full Film occurred approximately a year after Ms. Kaffka had
received the cease-and-desist notification from the claimants’ lawyer. It was
also several weeks after the Civil Resolution Tribunal issued its decision on
May 22, 2018. The email that Ms. Kaffka sent was addressed to the cast and crew.
Based on that email, it appears the link was sent to 23 people. It is not clear
how many people actually viewed it on her Facebook page.

[
319
]

Ms. Kaffka’s justification/explanation was that
it was only cast and crew members who could view the Film. It was password
protected on both platforms. Further, Ms. Kaffka believed she was acting within
her rights as a director to post certain behind the scene photos on social
media.

[
320
]

If the posting had been made immediately after
the Film was shot and before the dispute went to the Civil Resolution Tribunal,
Ms. Kaffka’s explanation might provide a defensible rationale. However, by the
point that Ms. Kaffka sent out her email on

June 4
,
2018, and
made the Film available to cast/crew, it was clear that copyright ownership was
in dispute. Moreover, by that point a decision had been made at the Civil
Resolution Tribunal in favour of the claimants. Whether or not this was known
by Ms. Kaffka at the time is not clear. This is not a case where the Film was
shared with one or two people. It was shared with a group of people and posted in
a relatively public setting, albeit with privacy settings. Nevertheless, in the
circumstances, I conclude that screening/posting the Film as Ms. Kaffka did, on
password protected Vimeo and Facebook platforms, constitutes a copyright
infringement under the
Act
.

Posting the Film

[
321
]

The claimants relied on a number of documents
which they said established that the Film had been posted in contravention of
the
Act
. By that I assume they meant it had been made publicly available
on social media. For ease of reference, I will address the documents by reference
to the section numbers listed in the claimants’ exhibit binder.

[
322
]

Section I - Google screenshots -
In her direct evidence Ms. Whitehall reviewed a number of Google
printouts. Ms. Whitehall

testified all those documents
were screenshots from a Google search of the Film name she conducted herself.
She said the 12 pages of Google screenshots showed Ms. Kaffka submitted an
unauthorized director’s cut to several websites using the name Whitehall
Entertainment. Ms. Whitehall’s objection, in part, was that she had never seen
the director’s cut. Moreover, she said her company was solely responsible for
marketing and promotion.

[
323
]

My review of the Google screenshots in section I
apparently taken 2018-05-24 (the date on the exhibit copy was cut off), leads
me to conclude that it is not possible by simply relying on the screenshots to
determine who, how, or why the information in the screenshots was placed on various
sites. The defendants suggested to Ms. Whitehall that these might be bot
generated references. I need not decide that. One of the issues with the
claimants’ documentary evidence of the Google search screenshots is that it is
hearsay evidence and thus the authenticity of the information is not
ascertainable.

[
324
]

In this case I find there is no reliable
evidence that Ms. Kaffka was responsible for any of these postings. Moreover,
there is no reliable evidence about what was contained in the postings because
Ms. Whitehall did not open any of them. She said she could not access some of
the links (except the one for Netflix). Ms. Whitehall agreed she did not know
whether the Film was even on any of these websites, excluding Netflix. I find, therefore,
that no infringement was established in respect of the above noted screenshots
in section I.

[
325
]

In regard to the alleged Netflix screenshot, Ms.
Whitehall said she clicked on a page she understood to be from Netflix.
However, she later agreed the website she was on was New Hollywood full Movies
for free. This Court cannot tell from looking at the specific page Ms.
Whitehall referenced whether in fact it is from the Netflix website. Ms.
Whitehall did not try to go into that link because she did not subscribe to
Netflix. In cross-examination, she agreed she did not know whether the Film was
there. However, she had initially said that “the Netflix one had 3,000 views
which would suggest that it was available and posted online.” In
cross-examination, defendants’ counsel asked Ms. Whitehall whether she was telling
this Court that she believed Ms. Kaffka somehow got an 18 minute film
distributed by Netflix. She said it was a possibility.

[
326
]

Ms. Kaffka testified about the documents in
section I, which the claimants alleged proved infringement. Defendants’ counsel
referred Ms. Kaffka to a series of website uploads in section I. Ms. Kaffka
said she believed they were basically phishing/spam websites. Ms. Kaffka
testified that at no point did she ever upload the Film anywhere publicly. She
did not upload anything to the websites in that particular sections of the
claimants’ exhibits.

[
327
]

The test the claimants must meet is on a balance
of probabilities not possibilities. I conclude that the screenshots tendered in
section I, including the alleged “Netflix” screenshot, do not establish that
the Film was available, nor is there a shred of evidence that Ms. Kaffka was
responsible for any of those postings. Accordingly, I find infringement under
the
Act
was not proven in respect of any of the above noted screenshots
in section I.

[
328
]

In section I Ms. Whitehall also referred to several
pages, which contained information taken from a Facebook for Kafka Pictures. Ms.
Whitehall said one of those documents established that Ms. Kaffka had posted
two endings of the Film. Ms. Whitehall said she watched a 30 second video that
was displayed on that Facebook page. Ms. Whitehall testified that video showed
two quick endings of the Film. In cross-examination, Ms. Whitehall acknowledged
that several of the documents in that section of the claimants’ exhibits
purported to show they were posted by Kafka Pictures Inc. Ms. Whitehall agreed,
however, that she did not dispute that Kafka Pictures Inc. was only incorporated
in January 2019.

[
329
]

Ms. Whitehall had some issues with the
suggestion put to her that previously Ms. Kaffka was the sole proprietor of Kafka
Pictures and that when she updated her account after incorporating, it
retroactively backdated the name on everything. Ms. Whitehall disagreed because
the date stamp on one of the screenshots showed the date 3 – 22 – 2018 at 8:16
AM. According to Ms. Whitehall, this established that the document was printed
before 2019 when Kafka Pictures Inc. was incorporated. However, when she was
asked about that screenshot Ms. Whitehall acknowledged, contrary to what the
Court understood had been her earlier evidence, that this particular screenshot
of behind the scenes footage was taken by a friend of hers and not by Ms.
Whitehall.

[
330
]

I find that the documents relied on by Ms.
Whitehall in section I to establish that Kafka Pictures Inc. was responsible
for the postings cannot be attributed to Kafka Pictures Inc., which was not a
legal entity until January 17, 2019. Moreover, to the extent that one those
documents is linked to Ms. Kaffka, (she acknowledged posting a 30 second behind
the scenes video) I am not satisfied it constitutes an infringement. In
reaching this conclusion I have taken into account Ms. Kaffka's role as a
director and producer, as well as co-executive producer. I have also taken into
account evidence that Ms. Whitehall was aware of social media exposure and
encouraged cast and crew to post on social media. Moreover, if it did
constitute infringement, given that the posting was only 30 seconds long, such
infringement would be
de minimus
in nature, at best.

[
331
]

Section J - Alleged Kafka Pictures postings
- The claimants relied on

several documents in section J from
Kafka Pictures. A number of them appear to have no relation whatsoever to the
Film. Section J of the claimants ' exhibits is labelled Social Media use Kafka
Pictures Inc. The defendants conceded that there were a number of shots, which
contained the name Kafka Pictures Inc. However, that is all they conceded. They
did not agree that it meant anything.

[
332
]

In direct examination, Ms. Whitehall, entered a
number of documents which she believed lead to certain conclusions about Kafka
Pictures Inc. During cross-examination, Ms. Whitehall clarified that at least
some (if not all) of the documents contained in section J

of the
claimants’ exhibits were screenshots taken by a friend of hers. Ms. Whitehall
explained this had been a stressful experience for her. She found it
disheartening to see things online. She was getting upset by it and a friend of
hers offered to take care of collecting screenshots.

[
333
]

Following this clarification, I raised a concern
about documents placed before this Court, which were collected by a person who
was not called to testify. The concern was that the person who was testifying,
Ms. Whitehall, had no knowledge of when the images were captured, or the
circumstances, or whether the document was a screenshot, photograph, and so on
and so forth. I noted that I would deal with the weight to be given to this
documentary evidence in my decision.

[
334
]

I reflected on this matter after having heard
all the evidence. I appreciate that in Small Claims Court there is some
flexibility, at the discretion of the trial judge, regarding the nature of the
proceedings. However, it is important to note that the rules of evidence nevertheless
apply. In some cases, allowing hearsay evidence on certain matters, which are
not critical or not in dispute, may be permissible. However, in cases where a
party is leading hearsay evidence to counter evidence directly in dispute and,
moreover, is asking the Court to draw inferences from that evidence, it is best
to be prudent and follow established evidentiary rules. In the circumstances, I
can give no weight to the

documents found in section J of the claimants’
exhibit. Accordingly, I find the documents in section J do not establish an
infringement.

[
335
]

Section K - Use of Whitehall Entertainment
name -
Ms. Whitehall also testified about what she
called the passing off allegation, namely, that the defendants attempted to use
the Whitehall Entertainment name and Ms. Whitehall’s name. In doing so they
damaged the claimants’ reputation and linked the unauthorized cut of the Film
to the claimants. Ms. Whitehall testified about documents in section K, which
she viewed as examples of her production company’s name being used by the
defendants on social media.

[
336
]

One of the documents was an IMDb entry and the other
was a poster for the Film dated only 2018. However, Ms. Whitehall did not know
for sure who made the IMDb entry. Nevertheless, she maintained it was her
“understanding” that it was Ms. Kaffka. There was also the poster which Ms.
Whitehall said was created by Ms. Kaffka without her permission or input.

[
337
]

With respect to the two
documents in section K, I conclude the following. The claimants have not
established that the IMDb entry can be attributed to Ms. Kaffka. Accordingly, I
find no infringement was established. The poster will be addressed

below
in the section on marketing the Film and may be addressed in the section
dealing with the alleged tort of passing off.

[
338
]

Section P – Miscellaneous social media screenshots

-

Ms. Whitehall
referred to an additional eight pages of screenshots in section P of the claimants
exhibits.

One of the documents is a screenshot with a handwritten note
indicating it was taken June 17, 2018. Ms. Whitehall made that note herself.
She testified the screenshot was from Ms. Kaffka’s personal Facebook page.

on Vimeo.

[
339
]

In section P of the documents there is also a
page that shows a screenshot of a Twitter account for the Film. Ms. Whitehall
said she did not create that account. She believed Ms. Kaffka created it
because Ms. Kaffka had posted tweets on that account “promoting” the Film.

[
340
]

In section P there was also another screenshot
of an Instagram account. Ms. Whitehall said she did not create it. She believed
Ms. Kaffka had created it. There were also other pages that were apparently screenshots

Moral Rights Infringement

[

Ms. Whitehall maintains that Ms. Kaffka’s

rights infringement. In particular, Ms. Whitehall claims that Ms. Kaffka’s
unilateral decision to edit the Script and the Film without her authorization,
the creation of the unauthorized director’s cut of the Film, and Ms. Kaffka’s
distribution thereof constitutes an infringement of her moral rights.

[

]

Ms. Whitehall submits that by making

edits
to the Script and editing a cut of the Film without her authorization, Ms. Kaffka,
in her personal capacity and on behalf of Kafka Pictures Inc., infringed upon
Ms. Whitehall’s right to the integrity of the Script and Film to the prejudice
of Ms. Whitehall’s honour and reputation. Ms. Whitehall also submits that by
claiming, or at a minimum insinuating, that Kaffka Pictures Inc. is an owner of
the Script and/or Film, the defendant infringed upon Ms. Whitehall’s right to
be referenced as the author and owner of the Script along with her sister.

[
370
]

The defendants’ position in this regard is that
Ms. Whitehall’s moral rights are only infringed if the work is, to the
prejudice of its author’s honour or reputation
,
distorted, mutilated, or
otherwise modified.

[
371
]

Section 14.1 (1) of the
Act
provides that
the author of a work has the right to the integrity of the work and, in
connection with an act set out in s. 3 of the
Copyright Act,
the right
where reasonable in the circumstances, to be associated with the work as its
author by name. The moral rights granted by virtue of s. 14.1 of the
Act

are subject to the provisions of s. 28.1. That section provides that any act or
omission that is contrary to any of the moral rights of the author of the work,
in the absence of the author’s consent, is an infringement of those rights.
However, that broad statement is qualified by s. 28.2 which provides that the
author’s right to the integrity of a work is infringed
only
if the work
is (a) distorted, mutilated, or otherwise modified, or (b) used in association
with a product, service, cause or institution, to the prejudice of its author’s
honour and reputation.

[
372
]

In
Collett v. Northland Art Company
,
2018
FC 269
, Gleeson J. noted that the jurisprudence recognizes that an author’s
right to the integrity of the work includes not only a highly subjective
aspect, but also an objective element. The subjective aspect must be
established by the author. The objective element, the proof of which must also
be established by the author, requires an evaluation of the prejudice to that
author’s honour or reputation based on public or expert opinion.

[
373
]

In
Wiseau Studio LLC et. al. v. Harper et.
al.
,
2020 ONSC 2504
, Schabas J. noted it is common ground that the burden
is on the plaintiff to establish a breach of moral rights. He also noted that
moral rights involve a consideration of both the subjective views of the
plaintiff and objective evidence. In particular, the court said

moral
rights are not, and cannot be, determined solely on the feelings or opinions of
the creator of the work. It relied on
Maltz v. Witterick,

2016 FC 524
,
for the proposition that, in addition to an author’s own subjective evidence as
to how his or her honour or reputation has been affected, the assessment of
whether a distortion, mutilation, or other modification is prejudicial to an
author’s honour and reputation also requires an objective evaluation of the
prejudice based on public or expert opinion (See paragraphs 202 and 203).

[
374
]

In
Prise des Paroles Inc. v.

Guerin
Editeur Lte.,
[1995] FCJ No. 1583
, the court considered the
Copyright
Act
and, in particular, the issue of moral rights. Denault J. noted that to
be able to make a claim based on the right to the integrity of an author’s
work, the author must establish the prerequisites set out in s. 28.2 of the
Act
.
In other words, the author must show that the work was distorted, mutilated, or
otherwise modified to the prejudice of the author’s honour or reputation. The
court noted that an author is not required to prove prejudice to his honour or
reputation, instead he/she must prove that the work was distorted, mutilated,
or otherwise modified to the prejudice of the author’s honour and reputation. The
court concluded this nuance justified the use of a subjective criterion,
namely, the author’s opinion, in assessing whether an infringement is
prejudicial.

[
375
]

In that decision, however, Denault J. also
concluded that the assessment of whether a work has been distorted, mutilated,
or otherwise modified to the prejudice of the author’s reputation requires an
objective evaluation of the prejudice based on expert or public opinion.
The importance of the objective criterion
is reflected in the court’s comment at paragraph 28. After noting that the
assessment of whether a distortion, mutilation, or other modification was
prejudicial to an author’s honour or reputation required an objective
evaluation, the court said:

In short,
although the author has shown that his novel was substantially modified without
his knowledge and that he was shocked and distressed by this, the evidence has
not shown that, objectively, as required by section 28.2(1) of the
Act
,
his work was modified to the prejudice of his honour or reputation. Since this
has not been proven, the plaintiff is not entitled to
moral
damages.

[
376
]

In this case, although Ms. Whitehall candidly
acknowledged that she had not seen the Film, she asserts that her moral rights
as an author have been breached. However, other than her subjective evidence
there is little, if any, relevant evidence regarding how her honour and
reputation have been affected by the activities of which she and Whitehall
Entertainment complained. Moreover, and more importantly, there was no expert or
public opinion evidence placed before this Court that would meet the objective
evaluation of prejudice required to determine whether Ms. Whitehall’s moral
rights have been infringed or otherwise violated. Accordingly, in the absence
of such an objective evaluation, Ms. Whitehall has not established an
infringement of her moral rights under the
Copyright
Act. Therefore, her
claim in that regard is dismissed.

Legal principles regarding implied terms

[
388

In an earlier section of these reasons I
summarized some of the general principles relating to the interpretation of
contracts. At this juncture, I set out specific principles applicable to the
implication of terms into an agreement as that is one of the central
submissions made by the claimants.

[
389
]

In
M.J.B. Enterprises Ltd. v. Defence
Construction (1951) Ltd.,
1999 CanLII 677 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 619, Iacobucci J. for the Supreme
Court of Canada summarized the three circumstances identified in
Canadian Pacific Hotels Ltd.
v. Bank of Montreal
,
1987 CanLII 55 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 711, in which
terms
may be i
mplied
into a contract:

… (1) based on custom or usage; (2) as the legal incidents of a
particular class or kind of contract; or (3) based on the presumed intention of
the parties where the implied term must be necessary "to give business
efficacy to a contract or as otherwise meeting the 'officious bystander' test
as a term which the parties would say, if questioned, that they had
obviously assumed" (citation omitted). (See paragraph 27)

[
390
]

More recently, in
Kaban
Resources Inc. v. Goldcorp. Inc.,

2020 BCSC 1307
, Voith J., as he then was,
reviewed the principles governing the implication of a term into a contract. In
addition to identifying the three analytical routes by which a term can be
implied into a contract, he also reviewed additional principles that are
relevant, including the following: the onus lies on the party seeking to imply
a term into a contract to establish that term; the device of implying the term
into a contract is to be used sparingly and with caution; the presumption is
against the adding to contracts of terms which the parties have not expressed;
and an implied term cannot be inconsistent with the express terms of a
contract. Moreover, Voith J. referred to the parol evidence rule. He noted
that, although the rule is riddled with exceptions, it is established that the
evidence of a party’s subjective intention is never admissible as an aid to
contractual interpretation. (See paragraphs 84 - 87)

[

]

In
Bhasin v. Hrynew,
2014 SCC 71
, the Supreme Court of
Canada considered whether parties to a contract owe a duty of good faith in the
performance of a contract. The Court recognized that good faith contractual
performance is a general organizing principle of Canadian common law. Parties
to a contract are under a duty to act honestly in the performance of their
contractual obligations. In doing so, the Court recognized that there is a
common law duty which applies to all contracts to act honestly in the
performance of contractual obligations.

[
430
]

In

Pareto Capital Partners (2011) Ltd. v. DVRM
Investments Ltd.,

2020 BCSC 1570
,
t
he court
noted that
Bhasin
does not establish that good faith
performance is a free standing remedy for a case in contract. Instead, it is an
organizing principle. It amounts to a common law duty applying to all contracts
to act honestly in the performance of obligations. In reaching that conclusion,
the court in
Pareto
referred to paragraph 73 of the

Bhasin

decision
where Cromwell J., writing for the Court, noted that the
general duty of honesty in
contractual performance means simply that parties must not lie or otherwise
knowingly mislead each other about matters directly linked to the performance
of the contract. This does not impose a duty of loyalty or of disclosure, or
require a party to forego advantages flowing from the contract. It is a simple
requirement not to lie or mislead the other party about one's contractual
performance.

[
431
]

In
Kaban
Resources Inc.
,
at paragraph151, the court addressed the comments of
the
Supreme Court of Canada in

Bhasin
found at paragraphs
63, 65, 69 and 70

of that decision. I paraphrase those paragraphs below:

•

The organizing principle is simply that parties generally must perform
their contractual duties honestly and reasonably and not capriciously or
arbitrarily.

•

In carrying out his or her own performance of a contract, a contracting
party should have appropriate regard to the legitimate contractual interests of
the contracting partner. “Appropriate regard” does not require acting to serve
the other party’s interest in all cases. It merely requires that a party not
seek to undermine those interests in bad faith.

•

The principle of good faith is different from the much higher obligations
of the fiduciary. Good faith performance does not engage duties of loyalty to
the other contracting party or a duty to put the interests of the other
contracting party first.

•

Good faith may be invoked in widely varying contexts therefore a judge
must have a highly context-specific understanding of what honesty and
reasonableness and performance require in order to give a proper consideration
to the legitimate interests of both contracting parties.

•

In applying the principle of good faith, a judge must consider the
fundamental commitments of the common law of contract which generally place
great weight on the freedom of the contracting parties to pursue their
individual self interest. Pursuing those self interests, may result in causing
loss to another but is not necessarily contrary to good faith.

•

The development of the principle of good faith must be clear not to veer
into a form of
ad hoc
judicial moralism or “palm tree” justice. In

THE TORT OF CONVERSION

[

The claimants submit that Ms. Kaffka engaged in

ink and supplies. The claimants say that the tort of conversion is one of
strict liability and therefore it is no defence to say that the wrongful act
was committed by Ms. Kaffka in all innocence.

[
442
]

The defendants acknowledge that conversion is a
strict liability tort which involves a wrongful interference with the goods of
another, such as taking, using, or destroying the goods, in a manner
inconsistent with the owner’s right of possession. However, the defendants say
that Ms. Kaffka did not take, use, or destroy the Film in a manner inconsistent
with the claimants’ possession of the Film.

[
443
]

They say that at all times Ms. Kaffka referred
to the Film as a Whitehall Entertainment production. Ms. Whitehall was referred
to as executive producer and, along with her sister, they were referred as the
writers. The defendants claim that Ms. Kaffka had intellectual property rights
in the Film and was entitled to protect those rights by withholding the raw
footage of the Film until the issue of ownership had been resolved. They

for those that were used up during the filming.

[
444
]

The test for the tort of conversion is addressed
in
Boma Manufacturing Ltd. v. Imperial Bank of Commerce
,
1996 CanLII 149 (SCC)
, [1996] 3 S.C.R.
727. In that case the Supreme Court of Canada noted that the tort of conversion
involves a wrongful interference with the goods of another. Some examples of
the type of interference include, taking, using, or destroying the goods in a
manner that is inconsistent with the owner’s right of possession.

[
445
]

The tort of conversion was discussed in
Ast
v. Mikolas,

2010 BCSC 127
:

[125] The tort of conversion involves
the wrongful interference with another person’s chattels such as taking, using
or destroying the goods in a way that is inconsistent with the owner’s
ownership of or title to the goods. See:
Boma Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canadian

Imperial Bank of Commerce
,
1996 CanLII 149 (SCC)
, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 727 at para.
31
.

[126] The three elements that must be proven
to establish the tort of conversion are:

(a)  a wrongful act by the defendant involving the goods of the plaintiff;

(b)  the act must consist of handling, disposing, or destroying the
goods; and

(c)  the defendant’s actions must have either the effect or
intention of interfering with (or denying) the plaintiff’s right or title to
the goods.

[127] Conversion is a tort involving strict
liability where even an innocent third party recipient of stolen goods may
commit the tort of conversion. In
MacKenzie et al. v. Blindman Valley
Co-Operative Association Ltd.
,
1947 CanLII 249 (AB SCTD)
, [1947] 2 W.W.R. 443, [1947] 4 D.L.R. 687
(Alta. S.C.), cited with approval in
General Securities Ltd. v. Parsons
,

[1955] B.C.J. No. 22 (C.A.)
, Chief Justice Howson stated:

The principle under which the
liability for conversion is determined is stated in the headnote of the report
of the House of Lords decision in the
Fowler v. Hollins
case,
supra
,
at p. 169: “Any person who, however innocently, obtains the possession of the goods
of a person who has been fraudulently deprived of them, and disposes of them,
whether for his own benefit or that of any other person, is guilty of a
conversion, unless the possession was obtained by him as finder or as bailee,
or by purchase in market overt or from an agent, so as to be protected by the
Factors
Acts
.”

[
446
]

In a more recent case,
Pang v. Zhang,

2021 BCSC 591
, Watchuk J. reviewed the
Ast
decision as well as several
other decisions. She summarized the case law noting that the essential elements
of the tort of conversion are:  a wrongful act; involving a chattel; consisting
of handling, disposing or destruction of the chattel; with the intention or
effect of denying or negating the title of another person to the chattel. (See
paragraph 64) In that decision Watchuk J. also noted that it is not a defence
to conversion for a party to say that he or she was unaware of a fraud (that
was the source of the conversion in that case). The intention element in
conversion is not about intention to steal or commit fraud, but rather the
intent to assert some authority or dominion over goods that is inconsistent
with the rights of the true owner of the goods. (See paragraph 44)

[

]
