THE
TORT OF PASSING OFF

[
457
]

The claimants submit that Ms. Kaffka and Kafka
Pictures Inc. have engaged in the tort of passing off. The allegation is that
the defendants have engaged in actions that damage the reputation of Whitehall
Entertainment and Ms. Whitehall. The actions the claimants specifically refer
to are the distribution of the “unauthorized” cut of the Film to film festivals
and the posting of the Film online. The claimants maintain those actions would
lead members of the public to be deceived into thinking that the defendants had
the approval of the claimants for their actions.

[
458
]

The claimants submit that Whitehall
Entertainment had developed a reputation of goodwill, by the time Ms. Kaffka
engaged in the activities, in connection with the production of another Whitehall
Entertainment film,
The Curtain
. The claimants say that by using the
trade name, which I take to mean Whitehall Entertainment, in association with
the defendants’ use of the unauthorized cut of the Film, the defendants caused
or were likely to cause confusion in Canada about Whitehall Entertainment’s
association with Kafka Pictures or by passing off the unauthorized cut as being
associated with and/or approved of by Whitehall Entertainment.

[
459
]

The defendants submit that the common law tort
of passing off has been codified in s. 7 (b) of the
Trademark Act.

The defendants identified three necessary components of a passing off claim at
common law. The defendants submit that the claimants have not established the
three elements necessary to succeed in a passing off claim. In particular, the
defendants submit, the claimants have not produced any evidence to establish
that at the time the Film was produced there was a presence of goodwill in
association with the trade name Whitehall Entertainment.

[
460
]

The defendants further submit that giving
credits to Whitehall Entertainment was not a misrepresentation. The Film was
produced according to the agreement between Ms. Kaffka and Ms. Whitehall and
credits had been agreed upon in advance. Additionally, and more importantly,
because the Film was never viewed publicly or posted in a public forum, there
was no opportunity for the public to be deceived or confused. In summary, the
defendants say that actual or potential damage cannot be presumed because there
was no presence of, or harm to, goodwill or reputation in the industry at the
relevant time, nor was there any misrepresentation.

[
461
]

The test for the tort of passing off was
reviewed in
Greystone Capital Management Inc. v.

Greystone Properties
Ltd.
,
1999 CanLII 5690 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 514. In that case, the court said the tort of
passing off concerns misrepresentations by one party which damage the
reputation or goodwill of another party. Moreover, the case set out three
components necessary to succeed in a passing off action, either at common law
or pursuant to statute. Those three components are:

a)

The existence of reputation or goodwill at the
relevant time. This includes consideration of whether the plaintiff was
recognized by the trade name and whether the trade name was distinctive within
the relevant field of activity.

b)

A misrepresentation leading the relevant public
to believe there is a business association or connection between the parties.
This includes consideration of whether the defendants’ use of the trade name is
likely to deceive the relevant public. Any misrepresentation need not be
deliberate and proof of intent is not necessary. Evidence of likelihood of
confusion, leading to the possibility of a lost business opportunity is
relevant. However, the establishment of actual confusion is not required.

c)

Damage or potential damage flowing to the
plaintiff as a result of any misrepresentation due to loss of control over its
reputation is presumed. (See paragraph 27)

[
462
]

With respect to the existence of reputation or
goodwill, the claimants say that Whitehall Entertainment had developed a
reputation of goodwill at the time the defendants engaged in the activities. In
making this assertion the claimants rely on the evidence of Ms. Whitehall.

[
463
]

Ms. Whitehall in giving evidence testified about
her experience and the number of films she had undertaken. However, it is
important to remember that Ms. Whitehall was testifying with the benefit of
hindsight. At the time the Film was being shot,
The Curtain
was still in
post-production. Correspondence filed by the claimants between Ms
.
Whitehall
and the composer of the music used in
The Curtain
establishes that as of
July 20, 2019,
The Curtain
was at the final stage of the film
festival circuit. It did well on the circuit but did not generate any revenue.
On that date, Ms. Whitehall wrote to the composer to seek her permission to
post the film online. Ms. Whitehall emphasized that the posting was not for any
money generating initiatives. She also emphasized that the composer would not
receive any compensation, as short films rarely generate any revenue.

[
464
]

Whitehall Entertainment was new to the industry
at the relevant time. I accept the defendants’ submissions that Ms. Whitehall
was also new to the industry and Whitehall Entertainment was a nascent
production company. There is ample evidence to support those conclusions. There
were a number of occasions in her testimony when Ms. Whitehall testified about
being a newbie, being just a writer, and not being familiar with various
matters relating to the film industry. I am not satisfied that the claimants
have established there was a reputation or goodwill and/or that Whitehall
Entertainment was a recognized trade name. I am not satisfied on the basis of
the claimants’ evidence that Whitehall Entertainment or Ms. Whitehall has
established a reputation or goodwill will at the relevant time period.

[
465
]

With respect to misrepresentation, I conclude
that the claimants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that
there was a misrepresentation leading the general public and/or filmmakers and
people in the film industry to believe that there was a business association
between Ms. Kaffka, Kafka Pictures, and Whitehall Entertainment. In this
regard, I considered the fact that the references made by Ms. Kaffka were in
the main credits for the Film. Additionally, I considered that the Film was not
viewed publicly, as such, and was not posted in a public forum. In reaching
this particular conclusion, I have taken into account that Ms. Kaffka posted
the Film on Vimeo and on her personal Facebook page. However, in both instances
it was password protected and posted solely for the viewing of the cast and
crew who had worked on the Film and not for general public viewing.

[
466
]

I am satisfied on the evidence that the
references to Whitehall Entertainment were not such that they caused or were
likely to cause confusion in Canada with respect to Whitehall Entertainment’s
association with Ms. Kaffka and/or Kafka Pictures. Accordingly, the claimants
have not established their claim regarding the tort of passing off in regards
to Ms. Whitehall or Whitehall Entertainment. Therefore, their claim in that
regard is dismissed.

[
467
]

The claimants sought judgment of the maximum damages
allowable under this Court’s jurisdiction, which is $35,000. They set out the
individual bases for their damage claims with an explanation. I will use the
list contained in the claimants’ submission as a guide and address each of the
heads of damages sought by the claimants. As I have outlined the position of
the claimants regarding the various claims in the course of this decision, I
will not review their position at this juncture. As noted, I will rely on their

[
468
]

The defendants submit that if this Court finds
Ms. Whitehall as the sole author and Whitehall Entertainment as the sole owner
of the Film and determines that damages are payable then statutory damages
should be limited to $100. Moreover, the defendants submit that in the
circumstances of this case the maximum for statutory damages is $5,000. The
defendants submit that in addressing the issue of damages the Court should
consider that the Film was not produced for a commercial purpose or expectation
of revenue. Accordingly, there was no actual or potential loss that resulted
from any alleged infringement. The defendants also submit Ms. Kaffka acted
justifiably and in good faith while protecting her intellectual property rights
and the integrity of her creative contributions in and to the Film.
Accordingly, there is no basis/need to deter similar conduct in the future.

[
469
]

The defendants submit that the claimants have
not provided sufficient evidence to succeed in their other contractual or tort
claims. They say there is no actual or proof of potential loss or damage in
respect to those claims.

[
470
]

The defendants submit that the claimants have
not provided any evidence to support their allegations against Kafka Pictures
Inc., and those claims should be dismissed entirely.

[
471
]

The defendants submit that the claimants have
not produced any evidence to support a claim for punitive damages. They point
to the fact that the matter before this Court is a
trial de novo
.
Further, they submit that Ms. Kaffka pursued the remedies available to her
under the
Small Claims Act
and Rules, which she is entitled to do and
should not be penalized for doing so.

[
472
]

Pursuant to s. 38.1 of the
Copyright Act
,
a copyright owner may elect to recover statutory damages instead of damages and
profits which are provided for in s. 35 (namely, damages which the owner of the
copyright has suffered due to the infringement and profits that the infringer
may have made). Section 38 further provides a range of damages which may be
awarded. If the infringements are for commercial purposes the range is from
$500 to not more than $20,000. However, if the infringements are for
non-commercial purposes the range is $100 to not more than $5,000.

[
473
]

In the circumstances of this case, I am
satisfied that the proper range of damages to consider is that set out under s.
38.1 (1) (b), namely, the range for non-commercial purposes. The evidence
establishes that the Film was a low-budget independent project. There was no
reasonable prospect of the Film making any money or of marketing the Film for
commercial purposes. Ms. Whitehall testified that one of the reasons she made
this Film and the earlier film,
The Curtain
, was to build up her portfolio,
so to speak, in the hope of being able to obtain grants for future projects.
She had been told that a good stepping stone to apply for grants was to write
and produce short films. She also noted that the reason she wrote the Script
for the Film was as a homage to her uncle. In light of that, I am satisfied
that the Film was not made for commercial purposes. Moreover, I am satisfied
that any infringements, which occurred were also not for commercial purposes.

[
474
]

The case law indicates that the purpose of
statutory damages is intended to ease the evidentiary burden on a copyright
owner. Nevertheless, statutory damages are intended to compensate the copyright
owner for its losses and, as well, to deter future infringements. The case law
indicates that there should be some correlation or proportionality between
actual damages and statutory damages. See
Trader

Corporation v.
CarGurus
,
2017 ONSC 1841
.

[
475
]

In this case, in respect of the claims under the

Copyright Act,
I conclude that there was no breach with respect to the
Script. The reason for that conclusion is that Ms. Whitehall essentially gave a
licence to Ms. Kaffka to work on the Script and use it to make the Film. This
occurred even before Ms. Kaffka was offered the roles of director and producer.
I find on the basis of Mr. Kim’s expert opinion that there was no breach when
Ms. Kaffka made some alterations to the Script, on the run, on one of the days
when the Film was being shot.

[
476
]

I will now address the damages claimed. Any
damages awarded must be paid to the claimant Whitehall Entertainment within
four (4) weeks of the date this decision is issued.

a)         The
claimants request $20,000 in statutory damages pursuant to the
Copyright Act

in connection with the defendant’s commercial use of the Film. Alternatively,
they seek general and special damages with respect to the defendants’
infringement of the Film and the Script.

With respect to statutory damages, I am satisfied
that the proper range of damages to consider is in the range set out in the Act
for non- commercial purposes. Given that the Film itself was not going to
generate any monetary profits, arriving at an appropriate sum for damages will
be somewhat arbitrary. However, this court must do the best it can to find a
broadly equitable result. In the circumstances, I conclude that while I cannot
arrive at an amount with arithmetical precision, an award of $3,000 is
appropriate for statutory damages.

b)         The
claimants request $28,000 in special damages for the cost to re-shoot the Film
as a result of Ms. Kaffka’s refusal to return the footage of the Film.

For reasons explained under the section
dealing with the tort of conversion, I conclude this is not an appropriate
damage award. Accordingly, I decline to award any damages related to a proposed
re-shooting of the Film.

c)         The claimants
request $2,500 in general damages for breach of Ms. Whitehall’s moral rights.

I found there was no breach of Ms.
Whitehall’s moral rights; accordingly no damages are warranted.

d)         The claimants
request $933.49 in special damages with respect to the unreturned hard drives
and physical property of Whitehall Entertainment.

I have directed that the hard drives and
related Film footage be returned to Whitehall Entertainment via its counsel.
Similarly, I have ordered that the red dress and blouse be returned to
Whitehall Entertainment if it is still in Ms. Kaffka’s possession. Furthermore,
as explained in the reasons dealing with the tort of conversion, I found that
the alleged conversion of other physical property outlined by Whitehall
Entertainment was not sufficiently established at trial to permit me to find
conversion had occurred. However, because Ms. Kaffka refused to return the hard
drives and related Film footage it is appropriate to award special damages of
$500.

e)         The
claimants request $5,000 in punitive damages against Ms. Kaffka for breach of
her duty of good faith.

I have found that Ms. Kaffka did not breach
her duty of good faith. Accordingly, no damages are warranted.

f)          The
claimants request $10,000 in general damages in respect of the defendant
passing off a cut of the Film as being associated with Whitehall Entertainment.

I have found that the tort passing off was
not made out by the claimants. Accordingly, no damages are warranted.

g)         The
claimants request $20,000 regarding unnecessary expenses incurred by Whitehall
Entertainment under Small Claims Rule 20 (6) including legal fees.

Ms. Kaffka had the right to pursue what was
essentially a
trial de novo
in Small Claims Court after she received the
decision from the Civil Resolution Tribunal. The claimants have argued that she
made it difficult for them to serve her and suggested she was evading service.
I am not satisfied that was the case. I decline to award any legal fees in
respect of this claim or any damages regarding unnecessary expenses.

Claim against Kafka
Pictures Inc.

[
477
]

On July 29, 2019, the claimants filed a claim
against Kafka Pictures Inc. under file number 1964880. They claimed that Kafka
Pictures Inc. had generally infringed Whitehall Entertainment’s copyright with
respect to the Film pursuant to s. 27 of the
Copyright Act
. They also
claimed that Kafka Pictures Inc. refused to return raw Film footage shot on May
27 and 28 to Whitehall Entertainment and that Kafka Pictures Inc. created and
distributed the Film as a Kafka Pictures Inc. production.

[
478
]

Ms. Whitehall also claimed that Kafka Pictures Inc.
had infringed her moral rights pursuant to s. 28.1 of the
Copyright Act.

Moreover, Whitehall Entertainment claimed that Kafka Pictures Inc.’s use of its
trade name infringed Whitehall Entertainment’s rights pursuant to s. 7 of the
Trademark
Act. (
I note parenthetically that the
Trademark Act
does not fall
under the jurisdiction of this Court.
)
Additionally, Whitehall
Entertainment claimed that Kafka Pictures Inc. by using its trade name in
association with Kafka Pictures Inc.’s use of the allegedly unauthorized Film
cuts, had passed off the cuts as being associated with and or approved by
Whitehall Entertainment.

[
479
]

At trial the defendants filed a BC Company
Summary for Kafka Pictures Inc. It showed that the time and date of the search,
which was the basis for that Summary, was July 19, 2021. That Summary showed
that Kafka Pictures Inc. was incorporated on January 17, 2019. The director of Kafka
Pictures Inc. was listed as Ms. Kaffka.

[
480
]

In her evidence, Ms. Kaffka testified that Kafka
Pictures Inc. was not incorporated until January 2019. However, prior to that
she used a similar name, Kafka Pictures, before January 2019. She was using

[
481
]

My conclusion with respect to Kafka Pictures
Inc. is that, given the fact Kafka Pictures Inc. was not in existence at the

Counterclaim by Ms. Kaffka

[
482
]

Ms. Kaffka filed a Counterclaim both in her
Reply and in her amended Reply. Given the conclusions I have reached in this

SUMMARY OF CONCLUSIONS

[
483
]

This is a brief summary of the conclusions
reached on the various issues raised by the parties at trial. It is a summary
only
for convenience
of the parties. Therefore, it does not replace the complete
analysis on the various issues raised by the parties and addressed in this decision.

Copyright related issues

[
484
]

The claimants maintained that Whitehall
Entertainment owned the underlying Script that was adapted into the Film.
However, Ms. Alicia conceded in her testimony that Whitehall Entertainment was
owner of the copyright in the Script and she was not claiming ownership of the
Script.

[
485
]

The claimants asserted that the presumption set
out in s. 53 (2) of the
Copyright Act
is dispositive of the issue of who
is a copyright owner of the Film. I did not accept that submission.

[
486
]

The claimants asserted that Ms. Whitehall, the
principal of Whitehall Entertainment, granted Ms. Kaffka a licence subject to
two conditions, namely, that Ms. Kaffka would follow the instructions of Ms.
Whitehall and that Whitehall Entertainment would be the owner of the Film. I
found the claimants did not establish that Ms. Whitehall placed any conditions
on her offer when she asked Ms. Kaffka to perform the roles of director and producer
for the Film.

[
487
]

The claimants further asserted that they did not
give Ms. Kaffka permission to carry out certain activities. Accordingly, this
Court considered Ms. Alicia’s assertion that she was an author, co-author, maker
or joint venturer with respect to the Film. In this regard, I found that the
evidence did not establish that Ms. Whitehall had granted ownership or co-ownership
to Ms. Kaffka during the course of telephone conversations. However, I did find
that Ms. Alicia and Ms. Whitehall reached an agreement whereby Ms. Alicia would
receive co-executive producer credit for the Film. I further found that, Ms. Kaffka
and Ms. Whitehall worked collaboratively on the Film. However, I was not able
to conclude on the evidence that Ms. Kaffka’s contributions represented the
kind of exercise of skill and judgment that was required to be considered an
author or co-author of the Film. I also found that Ms. Kaffka was not a
co-owner of the Film arising from a common undertaking or joint venture with
Ms. Whitehall and/or Whitehall Entertainment.

[
488
]

Another issue considered relating to copyright
matters was whether the activities alleged by the claimants constituted
infringement under s. 27 of the
Copyright Act
. The Court’s conclusions in
this regard are set out in these reasons.

[
489
]

Ms. Whitehall, as the author of the Script,
maintained that Ms. Alicia’s participation in the various activities the
claimants enumerated amounted to a moral rights infringement. I found that
although Ms. Whitehall had the subjective belief that her moral rights had been
infringed, there was no expert or public opinion evidence placed before the
Court. Accordingly, the objective evaluation of prejudice was wanting. Ms.
Whitehall’s claim for moral rights infringement was thus dismissed.

Contract related issues

[
490
]

With respect to Ms. Kaffka’s roles and
responsibilities, I found that there were no specific discussions regarding the
actual duties Ms. Alicia was expected to perform as a director and producer. In
particular, I found there were no specific discussions with Ms. Kaffka that she
was responsible for obtaining written assignments from the cast and crew so as
to maintain a clear title for Whitehall Entertainment in the Film. I also found
that there were no specific instructions or directions to Ms. Alicia that she
was obliged to follow the instructions of Ms. Whitehall or obtain advance
permission to carry out her roles.

[
491
]

The claimants relied on evidence given by Ms.
Whitehall and Mr. Kim, who provided opinion evidence. The claimants
acknowledged there was no written agreement. However, they urged this Court to
find that an implied term of the offer Ms. Whitehall made to Ms. Kaffka was
that Ms. Alicia would provide and perform the types of services that are
typically provided by individuals filling the role of producer and director in
the film industry. I declined to rely on Ms. Whitehall’s evidence in this
regard. I further found that her subjective intentions were immaterial and
could not form the basis for implying terms into an oral agreement. I also
found that Mr. Kim’s evidence, although helpful on some points, could not be
determinative of what might be implied in this particular case.

[
492
]

I found that the claimants did not establish
that they had discussed with Ms. Kaffka the duty to obtain copyright releases
from the cast and crew or that she was otherwise directed to do so. Further, I
found that the claimants did not establish that in a short film production,
such as the one in issue, the duty to obtain such copyright releases would
normally fall within the purview of director or producer or, if it did fall on
Ms. Kaffka, that it was not carried out.

Good faith obligation

[
493
]

I concluded that Ms. Kaffka did not breach the
obligation of good faith. Moreover, I concluded that the
Bhasin
decision
does not establish a freestanding remedy for a case in contract on the basis of
a breach of good faith obligation Therefore, in the specific circumstances of
this case the activities alleged by the claimants did not result in a breach of
the obligation of good faith.

Tort of conversion

[
494
]

I concluded that the claimants did establish
that Ms. Kaffka converted two Toshiba hard drives which held the footage of the
Film. I directed the return of those hard drives and the Film footage contained
therein. However, I declined to award damages for the footage of the Film which
the claimants valued at $28,000, based on the asserted cost of re-shooting the
Film. The Film itself has little, if any, commercial value. The budget for originally
shooting the Film was in the $8,000 - $10,000 range. The evidence also supports
a conclusion that films of this kind rarely, if ever, make money or turn a
profit. Additionally, with respect to the return of various items, I directed
two items be returned, if they are still in Ms. Alicia’s possession. With
respect to the rest of the items, I found that the evidence regarding who had
them in their possession was murky at best. I declined to make a finding of
conversion with respect to those miscellaneous items referred to by the
claimants.

The tort of passing off

[
495
]

I concluded that the claimants had not established
that Whitehall Entertainment and Ms. Whitehall had established they had a
reputation or goodwill will at the relevant time period. I further concluded
that on the evidence I was satisfied the references to Whitehall Entertainment
were not such that they were likely to cause or did cause confusion in Canada
with respect to Whitehall Entertainment’s association with Ms. Kaffka and or Kaffka
Pictures Inc. The claim with respect to passing off was therefore dismissed.

Damages

[
496
]

I have reviewed the claimants’ claim for damages
above. I will not reiterate my conclusions in that regard in this summary.
